title: Flexible rubber with metal-like thermal conductivity achieved via hydrogen bonding engineering

paper_content.abstract: The ideal electronics packaging for next-generation wearable devices and integrated circuits would be a flexible material with high thermal conductivity of a metal. We report a liquid-metal polyurethane composite (LiMPuC) with a thermal conductivity of 23.42 W m-1 K-1 while retaining extreme stretchability. The performance arises from interfacial-chemistry–guided ordering of the polyurethane matrix and improved liquid-metal wetting. By modulating hydrogen-bond donor/acceptor densities in the thermoplastic polyurethane and grafting –NH groups onto eutectic gallium–indium (EGaIn) droplets, we create anchored, reconfigurable interfaces that (i) increase matrix chain alignment and intrinsic heat transport and (ii) promote stable, strain-tolerant thermal near-percolation of the liquid metal. Under large tensile strain, these coupled effects preserve high conductivity and deliver a flexibility figure of merit > 100. This chemistry-to-microstructure pathway, linking hydrogen-bond engineering with LM surface functionalization, provides a general strategy for designing flexible, high-𝜅 composites for advanced thermal management in emerging electronics.
paper_content.introduction:
The rapid advancement of flexible technologies, such as artificial intelligence (AI) robots1,2 and wearable electronics3-5, is driving an urgent need for advanced thermal management materials that seamlessly combine high thermal conductivity with mechanical flexibility. Effective heat dissipation is critical in these devices, especially under dynamic and variable conditions where both flexibility and thermal performance are paramount6-8. For instance, wearable devices require materials that can conform to diverse shapes and withstand continuous movement while efficiently dissipating heat. Flexible thermal bridges, made from soft, stretchable substrates, are ideally suited for these applications, ensuring both user comfort and device reliability. Similarly, in advanced integrated circuits, flexible thermal conduits are employed to transfer heat between different sections of electronic devices, accommodating mechanical deformation and thermal expansion while maintaining efficient thermal conductivity.

Despite these growing demands, integrating superior thermal conductivity and exceptional flexibility within a material remains a significant challenge (Fig. 1a). Conventional polymeric materials like rubbers are inherently flexible, for example, polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) exhibits a flexibility figure of merit (f )9 greater than 1. Despite their mechanical advantages, these materials are typically thermal insulators FoM with thermal conductivity (𝜅) values less than 0.3 W m-1 K-1.10 In contrast, metals and ceramics offer excellent thermal conductivity (𝜅 >1 5 W m-1 K-1 for materials like stainless steel) but are rigid, with f FoM values less than 0.0111. This stark contrast highlights a fundamental trade-off between flexibility and thermal conductivity in existing materials.

To bridge this gap, significant efforts have been devoted to create composites by incorporating rigid, thermally conductive microparticles, such as metals12,13, ceramics14-16, and carbon-based materials17-19, into flexible polymer matrices. While this strategy enhances thermal conductivity, it often compromises mechanical flexibility, particularly when the filler content exceeds the percolation threshold necessary for effective heat transfer20-22. Liquid metals (LMs), such as eutectic gallium-indium (EGaIn), present a promising solution. LMs combine high thermal conductivity (EGaIn:~26.6 W m-1 K-1, Galinstan:~16.5 W m-1 K-1)23 and fluidity23-25, which allows them to conform to deformable microstructures within polymeric matrices, potentially maintaining the composite's flexibility26-28. This concept was pioneered by Bartlett et al29, who demonstrated stretch-activated thermal conduction in PDMS/EGaIn composites (𝜅 = 9.8 W m-1 K-1 at 400% strain and ~50 volume fraction (vol%) LM loading). Building on this foundation, subsequent studies by Haque30, Bark31, and Herbert32 have systematically improved thermal performance by engineering droplet morphology, introducing covalent anchoring strategies, and applying post-stretch annealing. Most recently, Yu et al33 reported a record-high 𝜅 of 27.1 W m-1 K-1 at 300% strain and ~80 % vol% LM loading, by percolating bulk gallium through a porous elastomer scaffold. In short, current LM-thermosetting polymer composites achieve thermal conductivities of approximately 10 W m-1 K-1 (under strain) with a f of approximately 1, representing a significant advancement over rigid particle FoM embedded polymers with similar thermal conductivity but much lower flexibility34-37.

Despite these promising developments, existing materials still fall short of the demanding requirements for high-performance wearable devices and next-generation advanced integrated circuits electronics. These applications demand materials that combine the thermal conductivity of metals (e.g., exceeding 20 W m-1 K-1) with the flexibility of rubber (e.g., f FoM over 10, as seen in materials like EcoflexTM)38,39. The key limitation in current LM composites is the lack of strong interactions between particles, and the existence of chemically crosslinked polymer networks that "lock" LM particles in place. This chemically inert oxide layer does not actively participate in polymer network crosslinking, resulting in weak interfacial adhesion and mechanical confinement. As a result, LM particles exist like isolated islands within the matrix (Fig. 1b left), preventing the formation of effective percolation networks at low concentrations. To achieve effective heat transfer, LM content must be increased significantly, such as reaching 60 % volume fraction (vol%). At this concentration, the thermal conductivity improves to around 11 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, but the flexibility deteriorates, resulting in a low f of only 0.237. Alternatively, to FoM maintain a higher f (e.g. ~50), the LM content must be reduced to approximately 44 vol%, but this FoM sacrifice in LM content results in ineffective percolation, with thermal conductivity reaching only 1.2 W m-1 K-1 in the natural state and 2.6 W m-1 K-1 under strain31.

In this study, we present an approach that fundamentally overcomes these limitations by optimizing interfacial chemistry to enhance the interactions between the polymer matrix and the LM particles. By leveraging non-covalent interactions, specifically hydrogen bonding, we promote a connectivity-approaching (near-percolation) droplet arrangement under deformation, reminiscent of a “pearl-necklace” morphology (Fig. 1b, right). Importantly, we use the term near-percolation to describe a state of increased droplet connectivity and reduced inter-droplet spacing, rather than classical hard-contact percolation. At the same time, the dynamic nature of hydrogen bonding reinforces mechanically reconfigurable interfaces, enabling high thermal transport while retaining stretchability. Through this strategy, at only 46 vol% LM incorporation, we have developed a composite material exhibiting an unprecedented thermal conductivity of 23.42 W m-1 K-1, almost double that of current stae-of-the-art LM embedded polymer composites, which achieve 13 W m-1 K-1 at 70 vol% LM loading30. Equally striking, this composite achieves a f exceeding 100, surpassing performance limits of pristine rubbers and establishing FoM benchmark for flexible materials. This approach not only resolves the longstanding trade-off between flexibility and thermal conductivity but also paves the way for the development of advanced thermal management materials for high-performance wearable devices, integrated circuits, and other flexible electronic applications.

2.1 Design and synthesis of thermoplastic polyurethane (PU) matrix with tunable hydrogen-bonding density

To engineer the H-bonding network within PU elastomers and their composites with LM, a series of PU elastomers was synthesized with precisely tailored H-bonding capacity. The synthesized PU samples are labelled according to their actual hydrogen bonding density (HEBD). For instance, PU2.90 indicates that the HBD in this pristine PU sample is 2.90 mmol cm-3. The synthesis strategy involved selecting components that balanced functionality, segmental mobility, and mechanical performance.

Polytetramethylene ether glycol (PTMEG), with varying molecular weights (M = 1000, 850, 650, and w 250 g mol-1), served as the soft segment. By decreasing M w of PTMEG, we increased the density of hydrogen bond donors and acceptors (see Supplementary Note 1, Supplementary Table 5 and 6 for detail), thereby enhancing the potential for H-bonding. This strategy allowed precise control over the HBD and ensured tunable mechanical properties. Isophorone diisocyanate (IPDI) acted as the hard segment, forming carbamate (–NHCOO–) bonds that function as both H-bonding donors and acceptors. Additionally, 2,6-pyridinedimethanol (PDM) was employed as a chain extender, introducing extra carbamate bonds and increasing segmental mobility by creating free volume for chain movement40. The molar ratio of IPDI:PDM:PTMEG was fixed at 1: 0.63: 0.37 to ensure the complete reaction of all functional groups (Fig. 2a).

Fourier-transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy confirmed the successful synthesis of the PU elastomers (Fig. 2b). The disappearance of isocyanate (–N=C=O) and hydroxyl (–OH) peaks indicated the completion of polymerization, while the appearance of carbamate (–NHCOO–) and ether (–C–O–C–) peaks confirmed the formation of the PU network41. With synthesis confirmed, the focus shifted to controlling the H-bonding interactions within the PU matrix. In this system, only the amine hydrogen (–NH–) from IPDI served as the H-bonding donor, while multiple acceptors, including carbonyl (–C=O), imine (–C=N), and ether (–C–O–C–) groups, participated in H-bonding interactions (Supplementary Figure 4, Tables 7-9). Note that, FTIR analysis of these interactions revealed shifts in vibrational peaks corresponding to H-bonding, providing bulk-averaged measurements of bonding populations rather than localized interfacial values.42. For instance, the –C=O stretching peak of the free carbonyl group, typically observed near 1720 cm-1, shifted to lower wavenumbers upon forming hydrogen bonds with the –NH group. This red shift produced two distinct –C=O stretching bands: one at 1699 cm-1, corresponding to disordered hydrogen bonds, and one at 1667 cm-1, associated with more ordered hydrogen bonds (as illustrated in Fig. 2c)43. The pyridine ring within the chain extender (PDM) also contributed to hydrogen bonding interactions. When the –C=N group of the pyridine ring acted as a hydrogen bond acceptor, its stretching peak shifted to a higher wavenumber (around 1555 cm-1), compared to the non-hydrogen-bonded state at around 1532 cm-1.44 Similarly, the ether (–C–O–C–) groups from both PDM and PTMEG participated in hydrogen bonding. The C–O stretching peak shifted to a higher wavenumber when the ether group acted as a hydrogen bond acceptor45. For free ether groups, peaks were observed at 1102 cm-1 (for PDM) and 1025 cm-1 (for PTMEG), whereas hydrogen-bonded ether groups exhibited peaks at 1149 cm-1 (for PDM) and 1051 cm-1 (for PTMEG)46.

By fine-tuning the M of PTMEG, we precisely controlled the density of H-bonding sites, thus modulating w the PU's microstructure and molecular interactions. The HBD in the PU, varied from 2.9 mmol cm-3 to 5.0 mmol cm-3 (Fig. 2f, see Supplementary Table 10 and Supplementary Note 2 for detail). Higher HBD values corresponded to increased densities of available H-bonding donors and acceptors, indicating active participation in hydrogen bonding. For example, using PTMEG with an M of 1000 g mol-1 resulted in w hydrogen bond acceptor and donor densities of 7.31 and 3.16 mmol cm-3, yielding a HBD of 2.9 mmol cm-3. In contrast, using PTMEG with an M of 250 g mol-1 gave acceptor and donor densities of 12.39 w and 5.35 mmol cm-3, respectively, resulting in a HBD of 5.0 mmol cm-3. This controlled modulation of HBD is crucial for optimizing the composite's mechanical and thermal properties, as it directly influences the structural organization of the polymer network and its interactions with the embedded LM.

X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns (Fig. 2d) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) analysis revealed significant changes in the microstructure with increasing HBD. XRD analysis of PU samples with varying HBD showed distinct changes in their crystallization behavior. For low HBD values (e.g., PU2.90 with a HBD of 2.9 mmol cm-3), only a broad peak at around 19.7° was observed, corresponding to an interplanar spacing of approximately 0.458 nm. This broad peak is indicative of amorphous clusters with short-range order. As the HBD increased, sharp diffraction peaks emerged at 28.6°, 32.1°, and 40.9°, corresponding to interplanar spacings of 0.311 nm, 0.279 nm, and 0.221 nm, respectively. The intensities of these peaks increased with higher HBD values, suggesting the formation of well-ordered crystalline structures within the hard domains of the PU samples. This enhancement can be attributed to strengthened H-bonding interactions that promote organized packing of polymer chains47. Complementary DSC analysis (Fig. 2e) further substantiated these observations. The PU sample with a HBD of 5.0 mmol cm-3 (PU5.0) exhibited a distinct glass transition temperature (T ) around 110 ℃. This transition signifies a shift from an g amorphous elastomeric state to a more semicrystalline plastic state as HBD increases. The presence of a clear T at higher HBD indicates restricted chain mobility due to stronger intermolecular interactions g facilitated by hydrogen bonds48. The concurrent evidence from XRD and DSC analyses underscores the pivotal role of H-bonding in dictating the thermal and microstructural properties of the PU samples. By fine-tuning the HBD through controlled variation of the soft segment molecular weight, it is possible to significantly alter the polymer's microstructure—from amorphous to semicrystalline—thereby influencing its mechanical and thermal behavior. In particular, the development of more ordered microstructures enhances phonon transport, resulting in a significant increase in thermal conductivity, from approximately 0.26 W m-1 K-1 to 0.69 W m-1 K-1 as the HEBD increases (Supplementary Figure 9). These results are consistent with prior studies49, which demonstrate that strengthening interchain interactions via hydrogen bonding can substantially improve the intrinsic thermal conductivity of polymers. Together, these findings underscore the critical role of hydrogen bonding in regulating polymer microstructure and thermal transport. Moreover, we establish a foundational strategy for enhancing the performance of PU-based composites, which will be further explored in subsequent sections.

2.2 Preparation and characterization of liquid metal-polyurethane composite

To fabricate the LiMPuC, EGaIn droplets were incorporated at a fixed volume fraction of 46% into a PU matrix. Prior to embedding, the droplet surfaces were functionalized with 3-aminopropyltriethoxysilane (APTES), introducing –NH groups on the native Ga O surface (Fig. 3a). These –NH moieties serve as 2 2 3 2 hydrogen-bonding donors that strengthen interfacial adhesion and wetting between the LM droplets and PU. As a result, the droplets are more effectively stabilized against interfacial debonding and maintain small inter-droplet separations under strain, which facilitates the formation of high-connectivity thermal transport pathways during deformation.

The successful grafting of APTES onto the LM surface was confirmed by the characteristic Ga–O–Si vibration at 457 cm-1 (Supplementary Figure 3)50, resulting in robust interfacial adhesion between LM droplets and the PU matrix. The introduction of LM droplets profoundly reconfigured the internal H-bonding landscape of the composite, as evidenced by FTIR spectra (Fig. 3b-f). In particular, key acceptor peaks of the PU matrix shifted upon LM incorporation. For example, the –C=O···H stretching vibration redshifted from 1667 cm-1 in pristine PU to 1662 cm-1 in LiMPuC, while the –C=N···H vibration associated with pyridine rings was redshifted by ~10 cm-1 relative to the neat PU (Fig. 3c). These shifts are attributed to the formation of stable, double H-bond interactions—enabled by the higher binding energy of –NH groups (5–10 kcal mol-1) compared to the original –NH donors (2–4 kcal mol-1)51— 2 between the polymer’s carbonyl and pyridinic nitrogen sites and the incorporated LM interface.

Quantitative deconvolution of the FTIR data (Supplementary Figures 5-6 and Table 10) revealed that the total H-bond density (HBD ) in LiMPuC could be systematically tuned via the M of the PU’s soft total w segment (PTMEG) (Fig. 3h). As the PTMEG M decreased, HBD increased from 1.46 to 2.38 mmol w total cm-3, following a trend established in the pure PU matrix. While the HBD among polymer chains (HBD PU- ) increased monotonically with decreasing M of the soft segment, the HBD at the LM-polymer PU w interface (HBD ) displayed a non-linear behavior. For samples with moderately low M (850–1000 LM-PU S w g mol-1), HBD remained around 0.6 mmol cm-3. However, further reducing the soft segment M LM-PU w below 650 g mol-1 led to a sharp drop in HBD to ~ 0.3 mmol cm-3. This substantial decrease is LM-PU attributed primarily to intensified steric hindrance from closely packed hard segments52 rather than interactions involving the nitrogen lone pair electrons, which provide weaker and less accessible hydrogen-bond acceptor sites53. Although functionalized LM particles could theoretically form hydrogen bonds among themselves, their dispersion and encapsulation within the rigid polymer matrix severely restrict direct particle–particle interactions, making this mechanism negligible in our system.

X-ray diffraction (XRD) further corroborated the interfacial and hard-domain structural features of the composite. Upon incorporation of LM, a broad diffraction feature centered at ~35.2° with a weak shoulder near 41.9° emerged (Fig. 3g). Importantly, these reflections do not indicate any atomic-scale ordering of the liquid metal droplets. Instead, they are attributed to the native nanocrystalline gallium oxide (Ga O ) 2 3 skin naturally formed on the EGaIn surface. Specifically, the features at 35.2° and 41.9° are consistent with the (002) and (−402) planes of 𝛽-Ga O (ICDD PDF# 41-1103), respectively. The pronounced peak 2 3 broadening is expected for an ultrathin oxide shell with nanoscale thickness and limited crystallinity. Meanwhile, a broad peak at ~19.6°, also present in pristine PU, arises from the intrinsic short-range packing correlations of the amorphous PU matrix. The persistence of this amorphous feature after LM incorporation indicates that the polymer bulk remains largely amorphous. Any structural modulation is therefore localized primarily within hydrogen-bond-stabilized hard domains and the polymer interphase adjacent to the LM interface, rather than within the liquid metal phase.

A key finding of this study is the strong correlation between interfacial HBD (HBD ) and the LM-PU composite’s thermal properties. Increasing HBD enhanced both thermal diffusivity and heat LM-PU capacity, thereby improving thermal conductivity (Fig. 3i). At the LM–PU interface, higher hydrogen-bond density enables more effective interfacial energy storage by allowing reversible bond dissociation and reformation, which raises the thermal energy required to elevate the material's temperature. In addition, increased interfacial HBD enhances molecular coupling between the LM droplets and the polymer matrix, restricting local chain mobility and possibly promoting low-frequency vibrational modes. These combined effects facilitate the formation of more efficient thermal transport pathways. As a result, LiMPuC3.41—with an HBD of 0.64 mmol cm-3—achieved a remarkable thermal conductivity of 4 LM-PU W m-1 K-1 at just 46 vol% LM loading. This thermal performance significantly exceeds previously reported values for materials with comparable LM loading (e.g., 1.3 W m-1 K-1 at 50 vol% LM)29.

The mechanical properties were similarly governed by the H-bonding network. In particular, the composites’ elongation at break is dominated by the H-bonding interactions among the PU matrices. As the HBD increased, the composites transitioned from ductile regime (elongation at break > 700%) to PU-PU brittle regime (elongation at break < 10%) once HBD exceeded 2.1 mmol cm-3. By contrast, the PPU-PU introduction of well-engineered H-bonding interactions between the PU and LM markedly boosted the toughness, measured as the area under the stress–strain curve54. This toughness reached a maximum of 9.97 MJ m-3 at HBD ≈ 0.65 mmol cm-3 (LiMPuC3.41). This high toughness reflects superior LM-PU interfacial load transfer arising from robust LM-PU interfacial H-bonding (Fig. 3j).

Notably, the synergy between mechanical toughness and filler-mediated thermal enhancement, quantified by the composite’s thermal conductivity per LM volume fraction (𝜙), underscores a unique mechano-thermal coupling in these composites (Fig. 3k). By strategically tuning the H-bonding network, we achieved exceptionally high thermal conductivity at comparatively low filler loadings while maintaining elevated toughness. This outcome suggests that robust interfacial H-bonding can both enhance energy dissipation mechanisms under load and foster continuous, percolated heat transfer networks.

2.3 Exceptional thermal conductivity of LiMPuC under strain

To investigate the strain-dependent thermal behaviour of the LiMPuC, we developed a custom in situ experimental platform combining uniaxial tensile loading with steady-state in-plane thermal conductivity measurements55, in accordance with ASTM-D5470 (Fig. 4a, See Supplementary Note 3.2 for detail). The reliability of this setup was verified against benchmark materials: quartz (𝜅 = 1.47 W m-1 K-1), 304 stainless steels (𝜅 = 15.3 W m-1 K-1), and copper (𝜅 = 380 W m-1 K-1). Measured thermal conductivities deviated by less than 10% from standard values (Supplementary Figure 12), confirming the accuracy of our apparatus. In addition, we cross-validated the setup by comparing its results with those obtained by laser flash analysis (LFA) on the composite samples without stretching (Fig. 3i and Supplementary Table 20), which yielded an average deviation of 4.8%, further corroborating the measurement fidelity.

Under tensile deformation, ductile LiMPuC samples exhibited a marked increase in thermal conductivity along the stretching direction. Particularly striking was LiMPuC3.41, which reached a thermal conductivity of 23.42 W m-1 K-1 at 400% strain—an approximate six-fold enhancement over its unstressed state (Fig. 4b). Under identical strain conditions (e.g., 400% strain), samples with higher HBD demonstrate enhanced thermal conductivity (Fig. 4c) under the same filler concentration. This remarkable LM-PU improvement stems from the synergy between the deformable EGaIn droplets and the stretchable PU matrix (Fig. 4d).

To elucidate the underlying mechanism, the investigation commenced with characterizing the mechanical response of the PU3.41. Progressive tensile deformation promotes increased chain orientation and hard-segment packing coherence in PU, as evidenced by XRD. With increasing strain, the initially broad scattering evolves into a more distinct diffraction feature that shifts from ~28.07° to ~29.24°. We attribute this evolution to strain-induced ordering/packing of hydrogen-bond-stabilized hard segments (often described as quasi-crystalline or mesophase-like ordering), rather than the formation of fully developed lamellar crystallites in the polymer backbone. The peak sharpening and shift to higher 2θ suggest increased packing density and orientational coherence of hard domains under the strain-fixed protocol.56,57 (Supplementary Figure 15a). Concurrently, FTIR analysis revealed an increase in ordered hydrogen bonding, specifically carbonyl-acceptor interactions, from 0.67 to 0.87 mmol cm-3 between 0% and 400% strain (Supplementary Figure 15b and Supplementary Table 21). This improved ordering substantially elevated the PU3.41 thermal conductivity from 0.32 W m-1 K-1 to 1.09 W m-1 K-1, highlighting a direct quantitative relationship between hydrogen bond ordering and thermal transport (Supplementary Figure 15c, d). Thermal conductivity accelerated markedly as ordered HBD exceeded 0.80 mmol cm-3, approaching approximately 1.1 W m-1 K-1 at 0.87 mmol cm-3.

Direct in situ measurement of the matrix thermal conductivity during composite stretching was experimentally challenging. Therefore, FTIR spectroscopy was employed to quantify ordered HBD density in LiMPuC3.41 (46 vol% LM) at each strain level. Due to robust interactions between liquid metal droplets and the PU matrix, the ordered HBD significantly increased from 0.98 mmol cm-3 to 1.32 mmol cm-3 over the strain range of 0% to 400%, strongly implying significantly enhanced thermal conductivity of the PU3.41 matrix within the composite. The strain-induced reorganization of hydrogen bonds at APTES-functionalized LM interfaces increases donor/acceptor matching, enhances wetting, and anchors chain segments that transmit load and orientation into the surrounding matrix. The resulting reduction of inter- and intra-chain scattering, together with improved LM connectivity, elevates the bulk 𝜅 composite while preserving stretchability. This ordering-driven enhancement is consistent with the broader literature on highly oriented polymers, where extreme drawing yields conductivities from tens to >100 W m-1 K-1 (e.g., polyethylene (PE) nanofibers and drawn films) despite isotropic PE being ~0.2 W m-1 K-1.58,59

Incorporating –NH functionalized LM droplets into the PU matrix strengthens interfacial wetting and 2 adhesion through hydrogen bonding. These interactions stabilize the droplet–matrix interface and maintain reduced inter-droplet spacing and high local connectivity, thereby forming a percolation-like conductive structure within the composite. As tensile strain increases, droplets progressively elongate into spindle-like morphologies and preferentially align along the tensile direction, producing an anisotropic microstructure that supports directional, high-conductance heat-transport routes.

Crucially, the dynamic hydrogen-bond network acts as a reversible “binder” that suppresses interfacial debonding and prevents droplet isolation, preserving the percolation-like interconnected structure even under large deformation. This stabilizes the strain-induced droplet reshaping and alignment, and thereby increases the number and effectiveness of continuous thermal pathways at the mesoscale, leading to a pronounced enhancement of the effective thermal conductivity (Fig. 4e).

We note that droplet deformability can be limited below a critical size, where Laplace pressure may inhibit elongation even with improved wetting. In addition, at sufficiently high strain, rupture of the oxide skin and associated electrical percolation may occur in some formulations, consistent with our preliminary observation of LM extrusion beyond 400% strain in a subset of samples (e.g., LiMPuC2.90). A systematic, size- and strain-dependent study of these electrical effects will be pursued in future work.

Taking LiMPuC3.41 as an example, we demonstrate its remarkable softness and deformability (Fig. 5a), exemplified by its ability to bend to a radius of 1.5 mm. Fig. 5b further illustrates LiMPuC’s thermal performance under torsional twisting between two thermal sources (52 ℃ hot end and 23 ℃ cold end). Even in this deformed state, LiMPuC effectively transfers heat across the twisted junction, exhibiting temperatures approximately 10 ℃ higher than those measured for PDMS under similar conditions. Infrared imaging (Fig. 5c) provides additional evidence of LiMPuC3.41’s superior thermal conduction: when stretched, it surpasses stainless steel, PDMS, and its own unstretched state. These results highlight the capacity of LiMPuC to maintain efficient heat dissipation even under significant mechanical stress, thereby meeting the stringent demands of flexible thermal management applications. Collectively, these findings confirm that the hydrogen bonding within LiMPuC not only imparts mechanical adaptability but also preserves robust thermal pathways, making it an exceptional candidate for next-generation flexible heat-dissipation technologies.
paper_content.methods:
4.1 Materials.
Polytetramethylene Ether Glycol (PTMEG, M = 1000, 850, 650, 250 g mol−1), 2,6-pyridinedimethanol w (PDM), isophorone diisocyanate (IPDI, 99%), 3-aminopropyltriethoxysilane (APTES) was purchased from Adams, Dibutyltin dilaurate (DBTDL) catalyst, N, N-Dimethylformamide (DMF), were purchased from Macklin. Toluene was offered by Aladdin. Eutectic gallium indium (EGaIn, 75% Ga:25% In) was purchased from Zhenjiang Asian Electronic Technology Co., Ltd.

4.2 The Synthesis of PU.
We maintained a fixed molar ratio of IPDI: PDM: PTMEG at 1: 0.63: 0.37, To remove residual moisture, PTMEG was added in a dried glass vessel equipped with a mechanical stirrer. It was heated by an electrical heating jacket at 120 ℃ under vacuum for 1 hour. After cooling down to 80 ℃, IPDI (100 mmol, 22 g) was added into the vessel and stirred for 1 hour under argon atmosphere. Then, catalyst DBTAL was dissolved in anhydrous toluene and added into the above system. The chemical reaction was continued for another 3 hours. Afterward, anhydrous toluene was added to adjust the viscosity, followed by employing PDM (63 mmol, 8.75 g) powder as the chain extender to the system to complete the reaction at 80 ℃. It took about 10 hours until the –NCO peak in the FTIR spectrum disappeared. Detailed information concerning the composition and quantitative content of each component is provided in the Supplementary Table 4. Finally, the mixture in the vessel was transferred into a rectangular mold and brought to vaporize the solvent in a fume hood at ambient conditions for 24 hours. The product was dried at 80 ℃ for another 24 hours in an air-circulating oven, followed by removing residual solvent at 80 ℃ for 24 hours in a vacuum oven.

4.3 Surface modification of liquid metal.
The surface modification of the liquid metal was carried out using APTES, which was pretreated by adding 10 mL of dimethylethanolamine (DMEA) to 110 mL of APTES to achieve an alkaline pH. 1.57 mL (10 g) of liquid metal was mixed with DMEA modified APTES (0.46 mL, 0.44 g) and DMF (1 mL, 0.95 g) to regulate the suspension’s viscosity. The resulting dispersion was subjected to magnetic agitation at 1200 rpm for 4 minutes at ambient temperature, whereby the bulk metal was comminuted into droplets with an average diameter of ≈10 µm. Subsequently, the stirring speed was reduced to 300 rpm and maintained for 2 hours, during which APTES hydrolysis proceeded and the silane was covalently grafted onto the droplet surfaces. The specific content of each component is provided in the Supplementary Table 11. The liquid metal suspension was then placed in a water bath ultrasonic device for 30 minutes to further reduce the droplet diameter to 1.52 m ± 1.17 m (Supplementary Figure 32).

4.4 Preparation of LiMPuC.
A separately, 1.68 g of PU was added to 5.07 g of DMF and stirred magnetically at 80 ℃ for 4 hours until completely dissolved. The PU/DMF solution was combined with the liquid metal/APTES suspension and stirred using a planetary mixer at 1600 rpm for 10 minutes. The liquid metal droplets were reduced to approximately 1 m by treating the mixture with an ultrasonic device in a water bath for 30 minutes. The mixture was then poured into molds pre-sprayed with release agent and dried at 80 ℃ for 24 hours.

4.5 Materials characterizations
1H Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (1H NMR) was recorded at room temperature using a 500 MHz NMR spectrometer (AVANCE Ⅲ, Bruker, U.S.) with dichloromethane-D as the solvent. 2 Attenuated Total Reflectance Fourier Transform Infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectra were acquired on a Vertex 70 spectrometer (Bruker, U.S.) equipped with a diamond ATR crystal. The wavenumber range was set from 4000 to 400 cm-1, with 64 scans collected at a resolution of 4 cm-1. X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were obtained using a D8 Advance diffractometer (Miniflex 600, Rigaku, Japan) with Cu Kα radiation (𝜆 = 0.1541 nm). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was performed on a field-emission scanning electron microscope (SU8010, Hitachi, Japan) at an acceleration voltage of 14 kV to analyze the sample morphology. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) curves were measured using a DSC25 analyzer (DSC25, TA Instruments, U.S.) under a dry nitrogen atmosphere, with a temperature range of 20–200 ℃ and a heating rate of 10 °C min-1. Modulated Differential Scanning Calorimetry (MDSC) was employed to determine the heat capacity at room temperature, with a heating rate of 2 ℃ min-1 across a temperature range of 17–30 ℃. The thermal conductivity of the samples in the unstretched state was measured at room temperature using a laser flash apparatus (LFA 467, NETZSCH, Germany) equipped with an out-of-plane fixture. For samples under tensile strain, measurements were performed using a steady-state thermal conductivity testing apparatus.

This manuscript reports a LM droplet-dopted elastomer composite. The authors claim that they achieve a streatching-enabled high thermal conductivity of 23.4 W/mK@400% for ϕ_EGaIn=46 vol% LM concentration, which violates the theoretical value of the parallel rule for the effective thermal conductivity: K_eff =ϕE_GaIn*K_EGaIn + (1-ϕ_EGaIn)*K_PL≈0.46*28+0.54*0.2=13W/mK (EGaIn is used here K_EGaIn= 28W/mK). The authores have no explanation about this unpredictable performance. Therefore, I cannot recommend this work publication in Nature Communications. The detailed issues including:

Soft materials, such as plastics and elastomers, are typically characterized by low thermal conductivity, while stiff materials, such as ceramics and metals, tend to exhibit high thermal conductivity. By delivering metal-like heat transport within a rubbery matrix at a moderate filler fraction of 46 vol%, this composite surpasses the existing performance plateau (10-13 W m-1 K-1) observed in liquid metal composites. The authors propose a hydrogen-bond–mediated interfacial design that simultaneously enhances LM percolation and strengthens the polymer network, thus overcoming the traditional stiffness–conductivity trade-off. I would like to raise comments regarding whether the reported thermal conductivity (23.4 W/mK) at 400% strain is reasonable.
Using the Voigt (parallel) model, the theoretical upper bound appears to be around 19.48 W/mK, assuming the thermal conductivity of the polymer matrix is 1.2 W W/mK at 400% strain. However, the authors provided data (Figure R2-1a and c) showing that at 400% strain, the ordered hydrogen bonding densities (HBDs) differ significantly between pure PU and PU/LM composites. Since the thermal conductivity of the PU matrix is strongly dependent on the degree of ordered HBD, the PU matrix within the composites at 400% strain is likely to have a value higher than 1.2 W/mK. This explanation is reasonable and quite interesting. Gallium-based liquid metals are known to oxidize easily under ambient conditions, and the polar oxygen-containing functional groups at the LM surface may indeed promote the formation of ordered hydrogen bonding in PU macromolecules during uniaxial stretching.
Nevertheless, I suggest that the authors delete the data in Figure R2-1b and d, and revise Table R2-2 accordingly. In the revised manuscript, they used a fitting extrapolation method to predict the thermal conductivity of PU at high degrees of ordered HBD. Although the exponential model fits the data well at low HBD order, it likely loses accuracy at higher levels. For instance, in Figure R2-1d, the predicted thermal conductivity of PU with an HBD order of 1.3 exceeds 20 W W/mK, which is unrealistic.
Overall, I believe that the main issues raised by the reviewers have been addressed satisfactorily. After minor and reasonable revisions, I recommend the manuscript for publication in Nature Communications.

This work, describing the effect of modulating hydrogen bond density on mechanical and thermal properties of PU-LM composites is interesting and cites measurement of thermal conductivities significantly higher than those previously measured in literature. The method of modulating hydrogen bonding is straightforward and well described in the manuscript. My concern in the manuscript comes from the discussion of liquid metal participation in the hydrogen bonding particularly with respect to stretch and some of the experimental data (and corresponding assumptions) made in the document. The instrument that the authors created itself appears valid and the authors have included appropriate references and comparisons to standards to convince the reader that measurements are valid. The authors also state at what strain they start to external evidence of LM droplet rupture, which is a common problem with LM composites when measuring any kind of conductivity. My challenge with this work is that (1) the authors use measurements of XRD and FTIR under strain to justify claims of hydrogen bond rearrangement [the authors should make it abundantly clear in the manuscript that it is hydrogen bonds and not the liquid metal droplets themselves that are rearranging] however the methods for taking this measurement (i.e., how strain was applied and maintained and in what direction/orientation) are not described anywhere and (2) the only evidence provided by the authors of what is happening morphologically in the composite is in Figure 4d and Supp Figure 30, both of which are highly unconvincing.
Surrounding the discussion of Figure 4, the authors use the word “percolation,” but classically the term percolation is when conductive elements are physically touching one another such that there is a clear pathway. That is not the case with LM droplets as at 46vol% the droplets are encapsulated with oxide and have a polymer barrier between them. There isn’t a real percolation threshold for liquid metal droplets in general, and for this system with the PU hydrogen bonding is a dominant force in the conduction percolation seems like an incorrect term. In Figure 4d the authors attempt to make the reader see the percolation by highlighting droplets in the PU system in red (I assume this is highlighting since the caption doesn’t describe why some droplets are red while others aren’t in either the PU or PDMS image). It isn’t clear why these droplets were chosen since they are not consistently in conductive contact or at least anymore obviously isolated than the droplets in the PDMS sample. The cartoon below the unstrained images is misleading since there are certainly droplets in the PDMS sample that seem as close in contact as the droplets in PU and there are many large gaps between the LM droplets in the PU just from the naked eye. I similarly don’t understand the strained image. The concentration of droplets seems to have significantly dropped in the strained PDMS image but not the PU image. Unless there is rupture of the LM composite and the loss of LM, and assuming that the magnification was maintained constant, there is no reason for there to be a sudden large gap between the strained LM in PDMS while the PU strained images appear more crowded.
In terms of organization that may promote thermal conductivity, the authors cite a peak that develops at 200% strain in XRD around 28/29o as crystallinity in the PU (the reference [55] does not highlight this peak, so I am not sure how the authors know that this peak related to crystalline PU). The authors also cite XRD of LM-PU composites that have a peak at 35o with the argument that these demonstrate short term order of the LM droplets. This is related to increase in thermal conductivity at the unstrained state. (1) I can’t understand how the LM droplets could show any kind of order on the level of 0.255nm and 0.224nm interplanar spacing. (2) SEM images indicate no order, and basically look like any other LM dispersion. If the “order” refers to PU directly adjacent to the LM interface this should be made very clear. I can understand that FTIR measures bulk which has interfacial measurements essentially baked into them, but even with the current revisions the authors need to refine their language about what the LM is inducing in the polymer, what happens in polymer bulk, and what is actually happening to the LM itself.
I hesitate to suggest new experiments, but it would be of great use to the reader to understand what happens to one of these samples after the initial strain. Are all of these measurements (XRD, thermal behavior, FTIR, etc.) done under strain or when the material is relaxed? Are the increases in crystallinity and “rearrangement” of H bonds permanent (so that straining is essentially a manufacturing process) or does the material have to be under strain in order to achieve these results?
In sum, the authors comments to previous reviewers leads me to believe that the measurements as presented are credible and believable, but the authors description of the phenomenon that leads to the increase in thermal conductivity should be better described. As stated, the description of percolation as well as induced polymer changes that come with the inclusion of LM are confusing or seemingly inaccurate.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The ideal electronics packaging for next-generation wearable devices and integrated circuits would be a flexible material with high thermal conductivity of a metal. We report a liquid-metal polyurethane composite (LiMPuC) with a thermal conductivity of 23.42 W m-1 K-1 while retaining extreme stretchability. The performance arises from interfacial-chemistry–guided ordering of the polyurethane matrix and improved liquid-metal wetting. By modulating hydrogen-bond donor/acceptor densities in the thermoplastic polyurethane and grafting –NH groups onto eutectic gallium–indium (EGaIn) droplets, we create anchored, reconfigurable interfaces that (i) increase matrix chain alignment and intrinsic heat transport and (ii) promote stable, strain-tolerant thermal near-percolation of the liquid metal. Under large tensile strain, these coupled effects preserve high conductivity and deliver a flexibility figure of merit > 100. This chemistry-to-microstructure pathway, linking hydrogen-bond engineering with LM surface functionalization, provides a general strategy for designing flexible, high-𝜅 composites for advanced thermal management in emerging electronics.

---

## Introduction

The rapid advancement of flexible technologies, such as artificial intelligence (AI) robots1,2 and wearable electronics3-5, is driving an urgent need for advanced thermal management materials that seamlessly combine high thermal conductivity with mechanical flexibility. Effective heat dissipation is critical in these devices, especially under dynamic and variable conditions where both flexibility and thermal performance are paramount6-8. For instance, wearable devices require materials that can conform to diverse shapes and withstand continuous movement while efficiently dissipating heat. Flexible thermal bridges, made from soft, stretchable substrates, are ideally suited for these applications, ensuring both user comfort and device reliability. Similarly, in advanced integrated circuits, flexible thermal conduits are employed to transfer heat between different sections of electronic devices, accommodating mechanical deformation and thermal expansion while maintaining efficient thermal conductivity.

Despite these growing demands, integrating superior thermal conductivity and exceptional flexibility within a material remains a significant challenge (Fig. 1a). Conventional polymeric materials like rubbers are inherently flexible, for example, polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) exhibits a flexibility figure of merit (f )9 greater than 1. Despite their mechanical advantages, these materials are typically thermal insulators FoM with thermal conductivity (𝜅) values less than 0.3 W m-1 K-1.10 In contrast, metals and ceramics offer excellent thermal conductivity (𝜅 >1 5 W m-1 K-1 for materials like stainless steel) but are rigid, with f FoM values less than 0.0111. This stark contrast highlights a fundamental trade-off between flexibility and thermal conductivity in existing materials.

To bridge this gap, significant efforts have been devoted to create composites by incorporating rigid, thermally conductive microparticles, such as metals12,13, ceramics14-16, and carbon-based materials17-19, into flexible polymer matrices. While this strategy enhances thermal conductivity, it often compromises mechanical flexibility, particularly when the filler content exceeds the percolation threshold necessary for effective heat transfer20-22. Liquid metals (LMs), such as eutectic gallium-indium (EGaIn), present a promising solution. LMs combine high thermal conductivity (EGaIn:~26.6 W m-1 K-1, Galinstan:~16.5 W m-1 K-1)23 and fluidity23-25, which allows them to conform to deformable microstructures within polymeric matrices, potentially maintaining the composite's flexibility26-28. This concept was pioneered by Bartlett et al29, who demonstrated stretch-activated thermal conduction in PDMS/EGaIn composites (𝜅 = 9.8 W m-1 K-1 at 400% strain and ~50 volume fraction (vol%) LM loading). Building on this foundation, subsequent studies by Haque30, Bark31, and Herbert32 have systematically improved thermal performance by engineering droplet morphology, introducing covalent anchoring strategies, and applying post-stretch annealing. Most recently, Yu et al33 reported a record-high 𝜅 of 27.1 W m-1 K-1 at 300% strain and ~80 % vol% LM loading, by percolating bulk gallium through a porous elastomer scaffold. In short, current LM-thermosetting polymer composites achieve thermal conductivities of approximately 10 W m-1 K-1 (under strain) with a f of approximately 1, representing a significant advancement over rigid particle FoM embedded polymers with similar thermal conductivity but much lower flexibility34-37.

Despite these promising developments, existing materials still fall short of the demanding requirements for high-performance wearable devices and next-generation advanced integrated circuits electronics. These applications demand materials that combine the thermal conductivity of metals (e.g., exceeding 20 W m-1 K-1) with the flexibility of rubber (e.g., f FoM over 10, as seen in materials like EcoflexTM)38,39. The key limitation in current LM composites is the lack of strong interactions between particles, and the existence of chemically crosslinked polymer networks that "lock" LM particles in place. This chemically inert oxide layer does not actively participate in polymer network crosslinking, resulting in weak interfacial adhesion and mechanical confinement. As a result, LM particles exist like isolated islands within the matrix (Fig. 1b left), preventing the formation of effective percolation networks at low concentrations. To achieve effective heat transfer, LM content must be increased significantly, such as reaching 60 % volume fraction (vol%). At this concentration, the thermal conductivity improves to around 11 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, but the flexibility deteriorates, resulting in a low f of only 0.237. Alternatively, to FoM maintain a higher f (e.g. ~50), the LM content must be reduced to approximately 44 vol%, but this FoM sacrifice in LM content results in ineffective percolation, with thermal conductivity reaching only 1.2 W m-1 K-1 in the natural state and 2.6 W m-1 K-1 under strain31.

In this study, we present an approach that fundamentally overcomes these limitations by optimizing interfacial chemistry to enhance the interactions between the polymer matrix and the LM particles. By leveraging non-covalent interactions, specifically hydrogen bonding, we promote a connectivity-approaching (near-percolation) droplet arrangement under deformation, reminiscent of a “pearl-necklace” morphology (Fig. 1b, right). Importantly, we use the term near-percolation to describe a state of increased droplet connectivity and reduced inter-droplet spacing, rather than classical hard-contact percolation. At the same time, the dynamic nature of hydrogen bonding reinforces mechanically reconfigurable interfaces, enabling high thermal transport while retaining stretchability. Through this strategy, at only 46 vol% LM incorporation, we have developed a composite material exhibiting an unprecedented thermal conductivity of 23.42 W m-1 K-1, almost double that of current stae-of-the-art LM embedded polymer composites, which achieve 13 W m-1 K-1 at 70 vol% LM loading30. Equally striking, this composite achieves a f exceeding 100, surpassing performance limits of pristine rubbers and establishing FoM benchmark for flexible materials. This approach not only resolves the longstanding trade-off between flexibility and thermal conductivity but also paves the way for the development of advanced thermal management materials for high-performance wearable devices, integrated circuits, and other flexible electronic applications.

---

## Results

2.1 Design and synthesis of thermoplastic polyurethane (PU) matrix with tunable hydrogen-bonding density

To engineer the H-bonding network within PU elastomers and their composites with LM, a series of PU elastomers was synthesized with precisely tailored H-bonding capacity. The synthesized PU samples are labelled according to their actual hydrogen bonding density (HEBD). For instance, PU2.90 indicates that the HBD in this pristine PU sample is 2.90 mmol cm-3. The synthesis strategy involved selecting components that balanced functionality, segmental mobility, and mechanical performance.

Polytetramethylene ether glycol (PTMEG), with varying molecular weights (M = 1000, 850, 650, and w 250 g mol-1), served as the soft segment. By decreasing M w of PTMEG, we increased the density of hydrogen bond donors and acceptors (see Supplementary Note 1, Supplementary Table 5 and 6 for detail), thereby enhancing the potential for H-bonding. This strategy allowed precise control over the HBD and ensured tunable mechanical properties. Isophorone diisocyanate (IPDI) acted as the hard segment, forming carbamate (–NHCOO–) bonds that function as both H-bonding donors and acceptors. Additionally, 2,6-pyridinedimethanol (PDM) was employed as a chain extender, introducing extra carbamate bonds and increasing segmental mobility by creating free volume for chain movement40. The molar ratio of IPDI:PDM:PTMEG was fixed at 1: 0.63: 0.37 to ensure the complete reaction of all functional groups (Fig. 2a).

Fourier-transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy confirmed the successful synthesis of the PU elastomers (Fig. 2b). The disappearance of isocyanate (–N=C=O) and hydroxyl (–OH) peaks indicated the completion of polymerization, while the appearance of carbamate (–NHCOO–) and ether (–C–O–C–) peaks confirmed the formation of the PU network41. With synthesis confirmed, the focus shifted to controlling the H-bonding interactions within the PU matrix. In this system, only the amine hydrogen (–NH–) from IPDI served as the H-bonding donor, while multiple acceptors, including carbonyl (–C=O), imine (–C=N), and ether (–C–O–C–) groups, participated in H-bonding interactions (Supplementary Figure 4, Tables 7-9). Note that, FTIR analysis of these interactions revealed shifts in vibrational peaks corresponding to H-bonding, providing bulk-averaged measurements of bonding populations rather than localized interfacial values.42. For instance, the –C=O stretching peak of the free carbonyl group, typically observed near 1720 cm-1, shifted to lower wavenumbers upon forming hydrogen bonds with the –NH group. This red shift produced two distinct –C=O stretching bands: one at 1699 cm-1, corresponding to disordered hydrogen bonds, and one at 1667 cm-1, associated with more ordered hydrogen bonds (as illustrated in Fig. 2c)43. The pyridine ring within the chain extender (PDM) also contributed to hydrogen bonding interactions. When the –C=N group of the pyridine ring acted as a hydrogen bond acceptor, its stretching peak shifted to a higher wavenumber (around 1555 cm-1), compared to the non-hydrogen-bonded state at around 1532 cm-1.44 Similarly, the ether (–C–O–C–) groups from both PDM and PTMEG participated in hydrogen bonding. The C–O stretching peak shifted to a higher wavenumber when the ether group acted as a hydrogen bond acceptor45. For free ether groups, peaks were observed at 1102 cm-1 (for PDM) and 1025 cm-1 (for PTMEG), whereas hydrogen-bonded ether groups exhibited peaks at 1149 cm-1 (for PDM) and 1051 cm-1 (for PTMEG)46.

By fine-tuning the M of PTMEG, we precisely controlled the density of H-bonding sites, thus modulating w the PU's microstructure and molecular interactions. The HBD in the PU, varied from 2.9 mmol cm-3 to 5.0 mmol cm-3 (Fig. 2f, see Supplementary Table 10 and Supplementary Note 2 for detail). Higher HBD values corresponded to increased densities of available H-bonding donors and acceptors, indicating active participation in hydrogen bonding. For example, using PTMEG with an M of 1000 g mol-1 resulted in w hydrogen bond acceptor and donor densities of 7.31 and 3.16 mmol cm-3, yielding a HBD of 2.9 mmol cm-3. In contrast, using PTMEG with an M of 250 g mol-1 gave acceptor and donor densities of 12.39 w and 5.35 mmol cm-3, respectively, resulting in a HBD of 5.0 mmol cm-3. This controlled modulation of HBD is crucial for optimizing the composite's mechanical and thermal properties, as it directly influences the structural organization of the polymer network and its interactions with the embedded LM.

X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns (Fig. 2d) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) analysis revealed significant changes in the microstructure with increasing HBD. XRD analysis of PU samples with varying HBD showed distinct changes in their crystallization behavior. For low HBD values (e.g., PU2.90 with a HBD of 2.9 mmol cm-3), only a broad peak at around 19.7° was observed, corresponding to an interplanar spacing of approximately 0.458 nm. This broad peak is indicative of amorphous clusters with short-range order. As the HBD increased, sharp diffraction peaks emerged at 28.6°, 32.1°, and 40.9°, corresponding to interplanar spacings of 0.311 nm, 0.279 nm, and 0.221 nm, respectively. The intensities of these peaks increased with higher HBD values, suggesting the formation of well-ordered crystalline structures within the hard domains of the PU samples. This enhancement can be attributed to strengthened H-bonding interactions that promote organized packing of polymer chains47. Complementary DSC analysis (Fig. 2e) further substantiated these observations. The PU sample with a HBD of 5.0 mmol cm-3 (PU5.0) exhibited a distinct glass transition temperature (T ) around 110 ℃. This transition signifies a shift from an g amorphous elastomeric state to a more semicrystalline plastic state as HBD increases. The presence of a clear T at higher HBD indicates restricted chain mobility due to stronger intermolecular interactions g facilitated by hydrogen bonds48. The concurrent evidence from XRD and DSC analyses underscores the pivotal role of H-bonding in dictating the thermal and microstructural properties of the PU samples. By fine-tuning the HBD through controlled variation of the soft segment molecular weight, it is possible to significantly alter the polymer's microstructure—from amorphous to semicrystalline—thereby influencing its mechanical and thermal behavior. In particular, the development of more ordered microstructures enhances phonon transport, resulting in a significant increase in thermal conductivity, from approximately 0.26 W m-1 K-1 to 0.69 W m-1 K-1 as the HEBD increases (Supplementary Figure 9). These results are consistent with prior studies49, which demonstrate that strengthening interchain interactions via hydrogen bonding can substantially improve the intrinsic thermal conductivity of polymers. Together, these findings underscore the critical role of hydrogen bonding in regulating polymer microstructure and thermal transport. Moreover, we establish a foundational strategy for enhancing the performance of PU-based composites, which will be further explored in subsequent sections.

2.2 Preparation and characterization of liquid metal-polyurethane composite

To fabricate the LiMPuC, EGaIn droplets were incorporated at a fixed volume fraction of 46% into a PU matrix. Prior to embedding, the droplet surfaces were functionalized with 3-aminopropyltriethoxysilane (APTES), introducing –NH groups on the native Ga O surface (Fig. 3a). These –NH moieties serve as 2 2 3 2 hydrogen-bonding donors that strengthen interfacial adhesion and wetting between the LM droplets and PU. As a result, the droplets are more effectively stabilized against interfacial debonding and maintain small inter-droplet separations under strain, which facilitates the formation of high-connectivity thermal transport pathways during deformation.

The successful grafting of APTES onto the LM surface was confirmed by the characteristic Ga–O–Si vibration at 457 cm-1 (Supplementary Figure 3)50, resulting in robust interfacial adhesion between LM droplets and the PU matrix. The introduction of LM droplets profoundly reconfigured the internal H-bonding landscape of the composite, as evidenced by FTIR spectra (Fig. 3b-f). In particular, key acceptor peaks of the PU matrix shifted upon LM incorporation. For example, the –C=O···H stretching vibration redshifted from 1667 cm-1 in pristine PU to 1662 cm-1 in LiMPuC, while the –C=N···H vibration associated with pyridine rings was redshifted by ~10 cm-1 relative to the neat PU (Fig. 3c). These shifts are attributed to the formation of stable, double H-bond interactions—enabled by the higher binding energy of –NH groups (5–10 kcal mol-1) compared to the original –NH donors (2–4 kcal mol-1)51— 2 between the polymer’s carbonyl and pyridinic nitrogen sites and the incorporated LM interface.

Quantitative deconvolution of the FTIR data (Supplementary Figures 5-6 and Table 10) revealed that the total H-bond density (HBD ) in LiMPuC could be systematically tuned via the M of the PU’s soft total w segment (PTMEG) (Fig. 3h). As the PTMEG M decreased, HBD increased from 1.46 to 2.38 mmol w total cm-3, following a trend established in the pure PU matrix. While the HBD among polymer chains (HBD PU- ) increased monotonically with decreasing M of the soft segment, the HBD at the LM-polymer PU w interface (HBD ) displayed a non-linear behavior. For samples with moderately low M (850–1000 LM-PU S w g mol-1), HBD remained around 0.6 mmol cm-3. However, further reducing the soft segment M LM-PU w below 650 g mol-1 led to a sharp drop in HBD to ~ 0.3 mmol cm-3. This substantial decrease is LM-PU attributed primarily to intensified steric hindrance from closely packed hard segments52 rather than interactions involving the nitrogen lone pair electrons, which provide weaker and less accessible hydrogen-bond acceptor sites53. Although functionalized LM particles could theoretically form hydrogen bonds among themselves, their dispersion and encapsulation within the rigid polymer matrix severely restrict direct particle–particle interactions, making this mechanism negligible in our system.

X-ray diffraction (XRD) further corroborated the interfacial and hard-domain structural features of the composite. Upon incorporation of LM, a broad diffraction feature centered at ~35.2° with a weak shoulder near 41.9° emerged (Fig. 3g). Importantly, these reflections do not indicate any atomic-scale ordering of the liquid metal droplets. Instead, they are attributed to the native nanocrystalline gallium oxide (Ga O ) 2 3 skin naturally formed on the EGaIn surface. Specifically, the features at 35.2° and 41.9° are consistent with the (002) and (−402) planes of 𝛽-Ga O (ICDD PDF# 41-1103), respectively. The pronounced peak 2 3 broadening is expected for an ultrathin oxide shell with nanoscale thickness and limited crystallinity. Meanwhile, a broad peak at ~19.6°, also present in pristine PU, arises from the intrinsic short-range packing correlations of the amorphous PU matrix. The persistence of this amorphous feature after LM incorporation indicates that the polymer bulk remains largely amorphous. Any structural modulation is therefore localized primarily within hydrogen-bond-stabilized hard domains and the polymer interphase adjacent to the LM interface, rather than within the liquid metal phase.

A key finding of this study is the strong correlation between interfacial HBD (HBD ) and the LM-PU composite’s thermal properties. Increasing HBD enhanced both thermal diffusivity and heat LM-PU capacity, thereby improving thermal conductivity (Fig. 3i). At the LM–PU interface, higher hydrogen-bond density enables more effective interfacial energy storage by allowing reversible bond dissociation and reformation, which raises the thermal energy required to elevate the material's temperature. In addition, increased interfacial HBD enhances molecular coupling between the LM droplets and the polymer matrix, restricting local chain mobility and possibly promoting low-frequency vibrational modes. These combined effects facilitate the formation of more efficient thermal transport pathways. As a result, LiMPuC3.41—with an HBD of 0.64 mmol cm-3—achieved a remarkable thermal conductivity of 4 LM-PU W m-1 K-1 at just 46 vol% LM loading. This thermal performance significantly exceeds previously reported values for materials with comparable LM loading (e.g., 1.3 W m-1 K-1 at 50 vol% LM)29.

The mechanical properties were similarly governed by the H-bonding network. In particular, the composites’ elongation at break is dominated by the H-bonding interactions among the PU matrices. As the HBD increased, the composites transitioned from ductile regime (elongation at break > 700%) to PU-PU brittle regime (elongation at break < 10%) once HBD exceeded 2.1 mmol cm-3. By contrast, the PPU-PU introduction of well-engineered H-bonding interactions between the PU and LM markedly boosted the toughness, measured as the area under the stress–strain curve54. This toughness reached a maximum of 9.97 MJ m-3 at HBD ≈ 0.65 mmol cm-3 (LiMPuC3.41). This high toughness reflects superior LM-PU interfacial load transfer arising from robust LM-PU interfacial H-bonding (Fig. 3j).

Notably, the synergy between mechanical toughness and filler-mediated thermal enhancement, quantified by the composite’s thermal conductivity per LM volume fraction (𝜙), underscores a unique mechano-thermal coupling in these composites (Fig. 3k). By strategically tuning the H-bonding network, we achieved exceptionally high thermal conductivity at comparatively low filler loadings while maintaining elevated toughness. This outcome suggests that robust interfacial H-bonding can both enhance energy dissipation mechanisms under load and foster continuous, percolated heat transfer networks.

2.3 Exceptional thermal conductivity of LiMPuC under strain

To investigate the strain-dependent thermal behaviour of the LiMPuC, we developed a custom in situ experimental platform combining uniaxial tensile loading with steady-state in-plane thermal conductivity measurements55, in accordance with ASTM-D5470 (Fig. 4a, See Supplementary Note 3.2 for detail). The reliability of this setup was verified against benchmark materials: quartz (𝜅 = 1.47 W m-1 K-1), 304 stainless steels (𝜅 = 15.3 W m-1 K-1), and copper (𝜅 = 380 W m-1 K-1). Measured thermal conductivities deviated by less than 10% from standard values (Supplementary Figure 12), confirming the accuracy of our apparatus. In addition, we cross-validated the setup by comparing its results with those obtained by laser flash analysis (LFA) on the composite samples without stretching (Fig. 3i and Supplementary Table 20), which yielded an average deviation of 4.8%, further corroborating the measurement fidelity.

Under tensile deformation, ductile LiMPuC samples exhibited a marked increase in thermal conductivity along the stretching direction. Particularly striking was LiMPuC3.41, which reached a thermal conductivity of 23.42 W m-1 K-1 at 400% strain—an approximate six-fold enhancement over its unstressed state (Fig. 4b). Under identical strain conditions (e.g., 400% strain), samples with higher HBD demonstrate enhanced thermal conductivity (Fig. 4c) under the same filler concentration. This remarkable LM-PU improvement stems from the synergy between the deformable EGaIn droplets and the stretchable PU matrix (Fig. 4d).

To elucidate the underlying mechanism, the investigation commenced with characterizing the mechanical response of the PU3.41. Progressive tensile deformation promotes increased chain orientation and hard-segment packing coherence in PU, as evidenced by XRD. With increasing strain, the initially broad scattering evolves into a more distinct diffraction feature that shifts from ~28.07° to ~29.24°. We attribute this evolution to strain-induced ordering/packing of hydrogen-bond-stabilized hard segments (often described as quasi-crystalline or mesophase-like ordering), rather than the formation of fully developed lamellar crystallites in the polymer backbone. The peak sharpening and shift to higher 2θ suggest increased packing density and orientational coherence of hard domains under the strain-fixed protocol.56,57 (Supplementary Figure 15a). Concurrently, FTIR analysis revealed an increase in ordered hydrogen bonding, specifically carbonyl-acceptor interactions, from 0.67 to 0.87 mmol cm-3 between 0% and 400% strain (Supplementary Figure 15b and Supplementary Table 21). This improved ordering substantially elevated the PU3.41 thermal conductivity from 0.32 W m-1 K-1 to 1.09 W m-1 K-1, highlighting a direct quantitative relationship between hydrogen bond ordering and thermal transport (Supplementary Figure 15c, d). Thermal conductivity accelerated markedly as ordered HBD exceeded 0.80 mmol cm-3, approaching approximately 1.1 W m-1 K-1 at 0.87 mmol cm-3.

Direct in situ measurement of the matrix thermal conductivity during composite stretching was experimentally challenging. Therefore, FTIR spectroscopy was employed to quantify ordered HBD density in LiMPuC3.41 (46 vol% LM) at each strain level. Due to robust interactions between liquid metal droplets and the PU matrix, the ordered HBD significantly increased from 0.98 mmol cm-3 to 1.32 mmol cm-3 over the strain range of 0% to 400%, strongly implying significantly enhanced thermal conductivity of the PU3.41 matrix within the composite. The strain-induced reorganization of hydrogen bonds at APTES-functionalized LM interfaces increases donor/acceptor matching, enhances wetting, and anchors chain segments that transmit load and orientation into the surrounding matrix. The resulting reduction of inter- and intra-chain scattering, together with improved LM connectivity, elevates the bulk 𝜅 composite while preserving stretchability. This ordering-driven enhancement is consistent with the broader literature on highly oriented polymers, where extreme drawing yields conductivities from tens to >100 W m-1 K-1 (e.g., polyethylene (PE) nanofibers and drawn films) despite isotropic PE being ~0.2 W m-1 K-1.58,59

Incorporating –NH functionalized LM droplets into the PU matrix strengthens interfacial wetting and 2 adhesion through hydrogen bonding. These interactions stabilize the droplet–matrix interface and maintain reduced inter-droplet spacing and high local connectivity, thereby forming a percolation-like conductive structure within the composite. As tensile strain increases, droplets progressively elongate into spindle-like morphologies and preferentially align along the tensile direction, producing an anisotropic microstructure that supports directional, high-conductance heat-transport routes.

Crucially, the dynamic hydrogen-bond network acts as a reversible “binder” that suppresses interfacial debonding and prevents droplet isolation, preserving the percolation-like interconnected structure even under large deformation. This stabilizes the strain-induced droplet reshaping and alignment, and thereby increases the number and effectiveness of continuous thermal pathways at the mesoscale, leading to a pronounced enhancement of the effective thermal conductivity (Fig. 4e).

We note that droplet deformability can be limited below a critical size, where Laplace pressure may inhibit elongation even with improved wetting. In addition, at sufficiently high strain, rupture of the oxide skin and associated electrical percolation may occur in some formulations, consistent with our preliminary observation of LM extrusion beyond 400% strain in a subset of samples (e.g., LiMPuC2.90). A systematic, size- and strain-dependent study of these electrical effects will be pursued in future work.

Taking LiMPuC3.41 as an example, we demonstrate its remarkable softness and deformability (Fig. 5a), exemplified by its ability to bend to a radius of 1.5 mm. Fig. 5b further illustrates LiMPuC’s thermal performance under torsional twisting between two thermal sources (52 ℃ hot end and 23 ℃ cold end). Even in this deformed state, LiMPuC effectively transfers heat across the twisted junction, exhibiting temperatures approximately 10 ℃ higher than those measured for PDMS under similar conditions. Infrared imaging (Fig. 5c) provides additional evidence of LiMPuC3.41’s superior thermal conduction: when stretched, it surpasses stainless steel, PDMS, and its own unstretched state. These results highlight the capacity of LiMPuC to maintain efficient heat dissipation even under significant mechanical stress, thereby meeting the stringent demands of flexible thermal management applications. Collectively, these findings confirm that the hydrogen bonding within LiMPuC not only imparts mechanical adaptability but also preserves robust thermal pathways, making it an exceptional candidate for next-generation flexible heat-dissipation technologies.

## Methods

4.1 Materials.
Polytetramethylene Ether Glycol (PTMEG, M = 1000, 850, 650, 250 g mol−1), 2,6-pyridinedimethanol w (PDM), isophorone diisocyanate (IPDI, 99%), 3-aminopropyltriethoxysilane (APTES) was purchased from Adams, Dibutyltin dilaurate (DBTDL) catalyst, N, N-Dimethylformamide (DMF), were purchased from Macklin. Toluene was offered by Aladdin. Eutectic gallium indium (EGaIn, 75% Ga:25% In) was purchased from Zhenjiang Asian Electronic Technology Co., Ltd.

4.2 The Synthesis of PU.
We maintained a fixed molar ratio of IPDI: PDM: PTMEG at 1: 0.63: 0.37, To remove residual moisture, PTMEG was added in a dried glass vessel equipped with a mechanical stirrer. It was heated by an electrical heating jacket at 120 ℃ under vacuum for 1 hour. After cooling down to 80 ℃, IPDI (100 mmol, 22 g) was added into the vessel and stirred for 1 hour under argon atmosphere. Then, catalyst DBTAL was dissolved in anhydrous toluene and added into the above system. The chemical reaction was continued for another 3 hours. Afterward, anhydrous toluene was added to adjust the viscosity, followed by employing PDM (63 mmol, 8.75 g) powder as the chain extender to the system to complete the reaction at 80 ℃. It took about 10 hours until the –NCO peak in the FTIR spectrum disappeared. Detailed information concerning the composition and quantitative content of each component is provided in the Supplementary Table 4. Finally, the mixture in the vessel was transferred into a rectangular mold and brought to vaporize the solvent in a fume hood at ambient conditions for 24 hours. The product was dried at 80 ℃ for another 24 hours in an air-circulating oven, followed by removing residual solvent at 80 ℃ for 24 hours in a vacuum oven.

4.3 Surface modification of liquid metal.
The surface modification of the liquid metal was carried out using APTES, which was pretreated by adding 10 mL of dimethylethanolamine (DMEA) to 110 mL of APTES to achieve an alkaline pH. 1.57 mL (10 g) of liquid metal was mixed with DMEA modified APTES (0.46 mL, 0.44 g) and DMF (1 mL, 0.95 g) to regulate the suspension’s viscosity. The resulting dispersion was subjected to magnetic agitation at 1200 rpm for 4 minutes at ambient temperature, whereby the bulk metal was comminuted into droplets with an average diameter of ≈10 µm. Subsequently, the stirring speed was reduced to 300 rpm and maintained for 2 hours, during which APTES hydrolysis proceeded and the silane was covalently grafted onto the droplet surfaces. The specific content of each component is provided in the Supplementary Table 11. The liquid metal suspension was then placed in a water bath ultrasonic device for 30 minutes to further reduce the droplet diameter to 1.52 m ± 1.17 m (Supplementary Figure 32).

4.4 Preparation of LiMPuC.
A separately, 1.68 g of PU was added to 5.07 g of DMF and stirred magnetically at 80 ℃ for 4 hours until completely dissolved. The PU/DMF solution was combined with the liquid metal/APTES suspension and stirred using a planetary mixer at 1600 rpm for 10 minutes. The liquid metal droplets were reduced to approximately 1 m by treating the mixture with an ultrasonic device in a water bath for 30 minutes. The mixture was then poured into molds pre-sprayed with release agent and dried at 80 ℃ for 24 hours.

4.5 Materials characterizations
1H Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (1H NMR) was recorded at room temperature using a 500 MHz NMR spectrometer (AVANCE Ⅲ, Bruker, U.S.) with dichloromethane-D as the solvent. 2 Attenuated Total Reflectance Fourier Transform Infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectra were acquired on a Vertex 70 spectrometer (Bruker, U.S.) equipped with a diamond ATR crystal. The wavenumber range was set from 4000 to 400 cm-1, with 64 scans collected at a resolution of 4 cm-1. X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were obtained using a D8 Advance diffractometer (Miniflex 600, Rigaku, Japan) with Cu Kα radiation (𝜆 = 0.1541 nm). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was performed on a field-emission scanning electron microscope (SU8010, Hitachi, Japan) at an acceleration voltage of 14 kV to analyze the sample morphology. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) curves were measured using a DSC25 analyzer (DSC25, TA Instruments, U.S.) under a dry nitrogen atmosphere, with a temperature range of 20–200 ℃ and a heating rate of 10 °C min-1. Modulated Differential Scanning Calorimetry (MDSC) was employed to determine the heat capacity at room temperature, with a heating rate of 2 ℃ min-1 across a temperature range of 17–30 ℃. The thermal conductivity of the samples in the unstretched state was measured at room temperature using a laser flash apparatus (LFA 467, NETZSCH, Germany) equipped with an out-of-plane fixture. For samples under tensile strain, measurements were performed using a steady-state thermal conductivity testing apparatus.

The ideal electronics packaging for next-generation wearable devices and integrated circuits would be a flexible material with high thermal conductivity of a metal. We report a liquid-metal polyurethane composite (LiMPuC) with a thermal conductivity of 23.42 W m-1 K-1 while retaining extreme stretchability. The performance arises from interfacial-chemistry–guided ordering of the polyurethane matrix and improved liquid-metal wetting. By modulating hydrogen-bond donor/acceptor densities in the thermoplastic polyurethane and grafting –NH groups onto eutectic gallium–indium (EGaIn) droplets, we create anchored, reconfigurable interfaces that (i) increase matrix chain alignment and intrinsic heat transport and (ii) promote stable, strain-tolerant thermal near-percolation of the liquid metal. Under large tensile strain, these coupled effects preserve high conductivity and deliver a flexibility figure of merit > 100. This chemistry-to-microstructure pathway, linking hydrogen-bond engineering with LM surface functionalization, provides a general strategy for designing flexible, high-𝜅 composites for advanced thermal management in emerging electronics.
